title: Bambara Groundnut and Finger Millet for Instant Complementary Foods: A Narrative Critical Review of Molecular Composition, Processing-Induced Chemical Changes, Functionality and Sensory Quality
content: Bambara groundnut (Vigna subterranea) and finger millet (Eleusine coracana) are underutilised African crops whose combination could improve the protein quality and micronutrient density of cereal-based instant complementary foods. This review examines the molecular constituents that determine their nutritional and technological value, as well as the chemical changes induced by processing. Bambara groundnut supplies lysine-rich protein and starch; nonetheless, its use is limited by phytic acid, phenolic compounds, a hard-to-cook defect linked to pectin–phytate interactions and cell wall lignification, and beany volatiles such as hexanal and 2-pentylfuran. Finger millet provides starch, calcium and phenolic acids, a large share of which are bound to cell wall polysaccharides, together with phytate and tannins that chelate minerals and bind proteins. Soaking, germination, fermentation and malting activate phytases and amylases, lowering phytate by up to 67% and finger millet paste viscosity from 1305 to 18 cP, while microwave and infrared heating gelatinise starch, aggregate proteins and shorten cooking time. Evidence for a finished product is limited to one instant porridge reported in a doctoral thesis. Future studies should link processing conditions to molecular outcomes, including phenolic and phytate profiles, starch and protein structure, volatile composition and in vitro digestibility, in a reconstituted Bambara groundnut–finger millet porridge
